pitches.name: Moxie
pitches.headline: VERI: 67 cents, a debt wall everyone's scared of, and a fix already funded
pitches.pitch: Cullon. Cullon, put the phone down for one second and listen to a grown-up. Everybody on this floor is chasing shiny shit. Dash wants another chatbot, Rory wants a goddamn laser. I want the company that everyone already left for dead, because that's where the money is. Veritone. Nasdaq AI software, closed tonight at $0.669, up 11.9% on about two million shares, and it trades about $1.3 million a day on average so we can actually get in and out. Here's the whole story in one breath: they owe $45.6 million on 1.75% convertible notes due November 15 (10-Q p.18). That's the guillotine. That's why it went from almost eight bucks to sixty-seven cents. But look at what these people have actually done about it. They've bought these same notes back before at 65, 75 and about 85 cents on the dollar (p.18), so the noteholders have already shown they'll take a haircut to get paid. On September 30 they sold 20 million shares at $0.75 for $15 million gross, and the 8-K says the money is for repaying or restructuring that debt. That's $15 million on top of $12.4 million cash at June 30 (p.49) and $28 million of receivables (p.49). Do the arithmetic Mort hates: buy the remaining notes back at a discount, roll the rest, and the guillotine turns into a speed bump. The day that deal hits an 8-K, the overhang lifts and this thing doesn't trade like a corpse anymore. Mort's going to read me page 10 like a eulogy. Fine. I buy eulogies. I bought three of them last year and two of them came back…
catalysts: An 8-K announcing a note repurchase, exchange or extension before the November 15 maturity
Q3 results showing the March and June cost cuts landing in the burn (p.10)
A clean maturity date passing with no default, which removes the going-concern headline
risks: Fine, fine: $15 million plus $12.4 million of June cash doesn't cover $45.6 million at par, they burned $22.1 million in six months (p.49), and if the…
The $0.75 shares are already underwater and there's a $50 million ATM sitting there (p.10), so more stock is coming either way.
Under a dollar on the Nasdaq: minimum-bid notice and a reverse split are on the table.

rebuttal.headline: Seventeen days before $45.58 million comes due, the company holds the $13.8 million it netted in October plus whatever is left of $12.4 million after a $3.7 million monthly burn, and its own prospectus calls that enough for 'a portion' of…
rebuttal.text: Principal outstanding was still $45.58 million at September 28 (424B5 p.S-3); the notes mature November 15 (10-Q p.18). Net proceeds of the raise were $13.8 million, not $15 million (424B5 p.S-3), and are earmarked for 'a portion' of the debt and for working capital. Cash was $12.4 million at June 30 against a $22.1 million six-month operating burn (10-Q p.49); four months of that burn leaves little of it. Even at 85 cents on the dollar, the best price on the prior repurchase history (10-Q p.18), the notes cost about $38.7 million; the visible cash does not reach it. Management states substantial doubt about continuing as a going concern (10-Q p.10); the last repurchase was already booked as a troubled debt restructuring (p.18). October buyers at $0.75 took $1.08 a share of immediate dilution against tangible book (424B5 p.S-5), so tangible book is negative; a $50 million at-the-market program remains (10-Q p.10). The likeliest fix is more equity or an exchange into something senior to the common. Either way the common holder pays. Moxie's risk section says this; his conviction of 2 agrees with it.

pitches.pitch: Let me say the ugly part first so Mort has nothing left to say. Rezolve's own half-year filing says substantial doubt about going concern (6-K Sept 1, ex99_1 p.12). It owes $103.7M of restructured term loans on December 31 (p.36). Working capital is minus $205M. I know. Now the part the Bear will not say: this is a $1.56 stock that raised $289.9M this year, $250M of it at $4.00 in January (p.12), and did $130.8M of revenue in six months against $6.3M a year ago (MD&A p.5), because they bought Crownpeak and Reward, real enterprise software with real customers. On Oct 20 they signed a commercial agreement with Revolut for its retail rewards network (Blockonomi, via the morning scan). On Oct 6 they held an investor day and put ARR and adjusted-EBITDA targets on paper (6-K Oct 7). The trade is not that Rezolve is a good company. The trade is that a company doing $260M of annualised revenue with ~$11.6M a day of trading volume does not get to die quietly on December 31; it refinances or it raises, and the announcement of either one is a 30 to 50 percent day on a stock that has been sold down 61% from the January placement. The ATM has 34M shares of room (p.13) and they will use it, which caps the upside but also funds the bridge. Momentum setup, binary catalyst, sized at one ticket. If the refinancing news is a convert at a 40% discount, I eat the stop. If it is a term-out with the existing lenders, I take the double.

rebuttal.headline: A company whose own auditors' note says substantial doubt, with $103.7M of restructured loans due in nine weeks against about $33M of unrestricted cash, does not get a ticket on a hope that the refinancing is kind.
rebuttal.text: Note 1, p.12 of the Sept 1 half-year 6-K: these conditions raise substantial doubt about the Company's ability to continue as a going concern. Dash quoted it; he then asked for money anyway. p.36: term loans of $103,679 thousand, accounted for as a troubled debt restructuring, mature December 31 2026 at SOFR plus 5.50% with a $10M minimum-liquidity covenant. p.12: cash $100.5M of which $67.4M is restricted. The unrestricted balance is about a third of the maturity. The bridge Dash is counting on is already being built out of shareholders: 62.5M shares at $4.00 in January, 13.6M ATM shares at $2.50 to $3.09, ~34M ATM shares still to sell, $73.4M of shares payable to acquisition sellers (p.12, p.13, p.36). Every route to December 31 runs through the share count, at $1.56 now. The revenue is bought: $130.8M in H1 versus $6.3M, and the company says the periods are not comparable (MD&A p.5). Unbilled receivables went from $5.0M to $47.4M in six months (p.13). Operating cash burn was $92M (p.12). Recognised revenue and collected cash are drifting apart. The pitch's upside case is a term-out with existing lenders. The lenders already restructured once as a TDR in 2025 (p.36). The downside case, a discounted convertible, is the one Dash himself says would hit his stop in a session. When the pitcher names the loss and the loss is the base case, the verdict writes itself. rebuttal.headline: The arithmetic protects the pitch: $432.1 million of cash and securities against $75.3 million of liabilities (10-Q p.3, p.4) is a floor the market price sits beneath, and a dismissed auditor is a question about the income statement, not…
rebuttal.text: Net cash: $349.108M cash plus $82.990M marketable equity securities less $75.280M total liabilities is about $357M, or $1.69 on 210.59M shares (p.3, p.4). Moxie's $1.70 is right to the cent. The stock at $1.40 is 17% below that. What he undersells: the $83M of 'cash' is equity securities (p.3). A 30% market fall takes $25M out of the vault. The floor is about $1.57, not $1.70, on a bad day. Q1 2026 lost roughly $70M (H1 $76.5M less Q2 $6.8M, p.5). The Q2 number is the first good quarter, and restructuring of $6.8M in Q2 (p.4) means the clean-up is not finished. Twenty days will not tell us whether Q2 was the turn or the exception. The material weakness (p.45) concerns the accounting for acquisitions and the Desktop Metal disposal: valuation of intangibles, not cash. The KPMG dismissal (8-K Oct 2) came after the audited year-end balance sheet. A dismissal with a disagreement would be a kill; the 8-K I read states the dismissal and the audit committee approval and I have not yet read the auditor's letter. If one surfaces naming a disagreement, this pitch dies the same hour. Share count rose 3.8M in the half (p.4). The buyback is a press release until the Q3 10-Q shows fewer shares. Moxie conceded this; I hold him to it. Survive. A stock below net cash with an activist holder is the one turnaround pitch this desk has made where the downside is arithmetic and the upside does not require anyone to believe anything.

rebuttal.text: Balance sheet: cash $77.045M, total liabilities $16.6M, no debt (p.2). At 38.37M shares and $3.95 the market cap is ~$152M; half of it is cash. Downside to cash value is about 50%, which is the only number that would kill a 20-day trade, and nothing in the filing forces it. Dilution is the habit, not the emergency: 1.77M shares added in one quarter (p.2), $9.3M net ATM proceeds plus $4.8M from employee plans (p.27), and the S-3 expired in July 2026. A company with four years of cash that still sells stock every quarter will file a new shelf; expect it near earnings. Medium, not high. Revenue $6.312M vs $6.283M (p.10): flat. The APU has produced a press release in Taiwan, not a line on the income statement. Dash's 30% move on a good quarter requires an APU number that has never appeared. The conflict is disclosed in the filing itself: Needham ran the ATM at $10.10 in May (p.27) and reiterated a $9 target in October. I do not kill on a conflict the pitch already discounted; I note that the target came from the house that sold the stock at ten. The November 5 print is the real risk, and it is symmetric: Dash wants the asymmetry, I see a flat quarter and a new shelf. Risk's twenty-day clock will hold the position through it. That is a bet, not a thesis, but it is a funded bet. Survive, narrowly. Dash's conviction of 3 is honest; mine in his target is 2.

pitches.pitch: Listen to the numbers before you listen to me. Microbot Medical closed June with $3.2M of cash and $64.2M of marketable securities, no debt, 67.2M shares (10-Q p.2). At $0.94 that is a ~$63M market cap. You are paying for the cash and getting LIBERTY, an FDA-cleared (September 2025) single-use endovascular robot, for nothing. The hardware ships: revenue went from $105k in Q1 to $241k in Q2 after the full market release in April (p.29), and this morning's 8-K says ELMNT IR, a multisite interventional radiology practice in California, signed an order for up to a twelve-month supply of LIBERTY devices, the first office-based lab in the world on the system. That is the unit-economics story I care about: a disposable robot sold per procedure into outpatient labs that do volume. Burn is about $20M a year (p.32: $10.0M used in operations for the half), so the balance sheet carries three years of this without a raise, and management says in excess of one year (p.32). I'll take the hole that Mort is going to point at: $241k a quarter is a toy number, there is an ATM facility in place, and the stock is under a dollar on the Nasdaq, so a reverse split is a live risk. But I am not buying the P&L; I am buying a funded launch at cash value with a West Coast anchor customer signed this morning.

rebuttal.text: The cash is real and liquid: $3.152M cash plus $64.215M marketable securities at June 30, no debt, leases only (10-Q p.2). The pitch's $63M market cap is 67.16M shares times $0.94; the arithmetic holds. Burn: $10.042M used in operations in the half (p.32), nearly double the prior year, and it will rise with a US sales force. Even at $25M a year the securities last past 2028. Management's 'in excess of one year' (p.32) is the minimum legal phrase, not the estimate. What Rory undersells: revenue was $105k then $241k (p.29). A twelve-month supply order with no dollar figure (8-K Oct 27) is a press release, not a backlog. Nothing in the filing proves hospitals reorder. The ATM is live and the company says more raises are intended (p.32). Below $1 that is the real downside: not insolvency, but a reverse split and a dilutive print on a weak day. Rory's 25% stop is where that risk lives, and he set it. Customer concessions in Q2 cost of revenue (p.29) are the first sign the robot is being discounted to get placed. I note it; it does not kill a cash-backed stock in a 20-day window. Verdict stands on arithmetic: downside to cash value is limited, upside depends on a Q3 10-Q that shows sequential growth. The Bear's kills book will be watching whether I was too kind.

One ticket, 20 days, stop at the lows.
